name: Acid-etched (satin, frosted) glass
process: One face of the float is exposed to a hydrofluoric-acid bath (the makers' recipes are their own) that dissolves the glass unevenly and leaves a uniform field of microscopic facets and pits: the face scatters light and loses its gloss while the glass beneath is unchanged. The etch is made on the flat sheet before any toughening, laminating or insulating, and the etched glass keeps its substrate's strength. The finish is set by the etch: from a light satin that still shows shapes behind it to an opaque, velvety white; the colour of the etch must match within Delta E* 2 between neighbouring panes, and slight 'clouds' of uneven haze are the typical defect. Walker describes its etched finishes as smooth, durable and resistant to wear and staining; sandblasting, the other way to frost glass, roughens the surface far more (see alternatives).

wetness.text: A water film on the etched face fills its texture with a liquid of index close to glass's and makes it partly clear; the etched face should face the dry side (inside) of the Elan's drum and roof.
wetness.derivation: Index matching: the reflectance of each facet falls from ((1.523-1)/(1.523+1))^2 = 0.043 in air to ((1.523-1.333)/(1.523+1.333))^2 = 0.0044 under water, so the scattering of the facets falls about tenfold

strength.text: 'For acid etched glass manufactured on float glass, coated glass, thermally toughened glass or laminated glass, the same value of mechanical strength shall be used as for the glass substrate.'

defects.text: Uniformity defects: 'slight visible variation in haze effect within a pane or from pane to pane ... (e.g. clouds)'; punctual defects from cutting-oil droplets or silicone; judged at 300-600 lux from at least 50 cm.

sandblasted.text: Sandblasting soda-lime glass raises its roughness Ra from 0.035 to 2.27 um as more sand is projected; the specular transmittance falls from 0.916 to 0.13 while the scattered transmittance rises to 0.81; the surface becomes visibly damaged beyond about Ra 1.5 um. It is not the museum's finish.
sandblasted.source: S. Benterki, C. Bousbaa, N. Laouar and A. Faci, 'Characterization of the sandblasted glass degradation by light scattering', Optik (2018), https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0030402617317734 (values from the abstract only)

fritted.text: A white ceramic frit fired on the glass (fritted) passes far less light (about 0.32) and scatters it almost evenly: a white glow rather than a bright satin.

carFloor.text: The car's floor: the glass instance at opacity 0.3, roughness 0.3, specular 0.5, tint (0.86, 0.90, 0.89), diffuse 0.08: 'a pale satin, so it reads as a floor you can see down through'.

asBuiltCorrection.text: The as-built misty glass is self-lit at a constant 450 nits scaled by a daylight factor. Physically it is glass that passes the sky's light and scatters it: an etched pane passes about 0.9 of it, spread over a wide cone; a white frit about 0.3, spread almost evenly; so its luminance follows the real sky behind it (and the sun's disc shows through an etched pane as a bright blur). Light should compute it from the sky and the record, never from a nits constant (principle 5: fix causes).
asBuiltCorrection.source: MuseeVision/Journal/Decisions.md, D-001 (the design is the finished museum) and D-017 (port the finished rooms; the as-built material values seed the records)

photograph: An etched pane lit by the sky is an even, bright satin with the sun as a soft glowing blur; shapes pressed against it show, those a little behind it vanish.
In reflection the etched face is matt; the smooth face still mirrors, so a pane seen from the smooth side shows a faint reflection over the milky glow.
Fingerprints and grease darken an etched face where it is touched (the car's rail height, the floor under foot).
